questions.stem: A competency assessment shows that staff can complete catheter-insertion steps correctly but often fail to respond when contamination occurs. What is the best programme redesign?

options.text: Include realistic contamination interruptions, immediate feedback and repeat practice until safe judgement is demonstrated.
Add more written theory about catheterisation.
Allow staff to self-certify after watching a video.

questions.rationale: Competence includes judgement and response to complications, not only completion of steps. Deliberate practice with feedback targets the observed gap.

questions.stem: Which element should a comprehensive clinical-skills competency framework assess?

options.text: Knowledge, preparation, technical accuracy, communication, judgement and evaluation.

questions.rationale: The notes emphasise that competence is multidimensional and cannot be reduced to a procedural checklist.

questions.stem: A learner performs a procedure correctly once during simulation. What should the educator do before confirming competence?

options.text: Sign off immediately because the steps were correct.
Ask the learner to complete a reflective paragraph only.
Assess consistency, reasoning, communication and response to complications through further supervised performance.

questions.rationale: One successful performance may not demonstrate reliable competence across conditions.

questions.stem: Which feedback statement is most effective?

options.text: You need to be more careful.
You are not ready for practice.
During sterile setup, your sleeve crossed the field; pause, re-establish the field and repeat the setup now.

questions.rationale: Feedback should be specific, timely, linked to observable behaviour and followed by another practice opportunity.

questions.stem: A nurse admits uncertainty about using a device and asks for supervision. What is the most appropriate educator response?

options.text: Support the request and arrange supervised practice before independent use.
Criticise the nurse for lack of confidence.
Ask the nurse to learn by trial and error.
Remove the nurse permanently from device use.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety makes help-seeking expected and prevents unsafe independent practice.

questions.stem: Which simulation scenario best develops clinical judgement?

options.text: A predictable procedure with no interruptions.
A procedure that includes changing observations, equipment difficulty and a decision about whether to stop.
A lecture followed by a quiz.

questions.rationale: Realistic decision points and complications strengthen judgement, not just motor performance.

questions.stem: A skills educator notices wide variation in how assessors judge the same performance. What should happen?

options.text: Allow assessor preference because clinical practice varies.
Use only one assessor for all staff.
Clarify standards, use agreed criteria and calibrate assessors using shared examples.

questions.rationale: Consistent criteria and assessor calibration improve fairness and reliability.

questions.stem: Which action best supports deliberate practice?

options.text: Reading the policy after an error.
Repeated focused practice of a specific weakness with feedback and another attempt.

questions.rationale: Deliberate practice is focused, repeated and feedback-driven.

questions.stem: A learner becomes defensive after feedback. What is the best coaching response?

options.text: Return to observable behaviour, invite reflection and agree on a specific practice goal.
Compare the learner with stronger colleagues.

questions.rationale: Constructive coaching remains specific, respectful and improvement-focused.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of a checklist-only competency assessment?

options.text: Checklists are too difficult to score.
They may confirm task completion without assessing reasoning, communication or adaptation.
They cannot be used in simulation.

questions.rationale: A checklist supports consistency but does not replace judgement.

questions.stem: A nurse repeatedly performs well in simulation but poorly during busy shifts. What should the educator investigate?

options.text: Whether the nurse prefers another specialty.
Transfer of learning, workload, interruptions, supervision and real-world conditions.

questions.rationale: Performance is shaped by both competence and workplace conditions.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates an effective skills programme?

options.text: Consistent safe performance, appropriate help-seeking and improved patient outcomes.

questions.rationale: Training should translate into reliable practice and safer care.

questions.stem: A mentor observes that a nurse understands theory but hesitates during complications. What is the best next step?

options.text: Use supervised complication scenarios with guided reasoning and feedback.
Avoid exposing the nurse to complexity.

questions.rationale: The identified gap is applied judgement under changing conditions.

questions.stem: Which environment most strongly supports learning?

options.text: One in which errors are hidden.
One in which uncertainty can be discussed without humiliation while standards remain clear.
One in which only experts speak.
One in which every error leads to punishment.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety supports honest learning and early help-seeking.

questions.stem: A competency programme uses the same assessment for novice and advanced nurses. What is the main concern?

options.text: All learners should be assessed identically.
Assessment may not match role, risk or expected level of judgement.

questions.rationale: Competency processes should align with role and clinical risk.

questions.stem: Which action best develops assessors?

options.text: Allow assessors to rely on intuition.
Train assessors, compare scoring decisions and review difficult cases together.

questions.rationale: Assessor preparation and calibration improve consistency.

questions.stem: A learner makes an error during simulation that would have harmed a patient. What should the educator do?

options.text: Use debriefing to examine reasoning, system factors and a safe repeat performance.
Ignore it because no patient was harmed.

questions.rationale: Simulation allows errors to become structured learning opportunities.

questions.stem: Which teaching method is strongest for a high-risk skill?

options.text: Demonstration, supervised practice, realistic simulation, feedback and reassessment.

questions.rationale: High-risk skills require multimodal practice and verified performance.

questions.stem: A nurse performs safely but cannot explain critical safety rationales. What should the assessor conclude?

options.text: Competence is complete because performance was correct.
Further assessment is needed because understanding supports adaptation to unexpected events.

questions.rationale: Verbalised reasoning helps confirm that safe actions can be adapted beyond memorised steps.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 3 leadership in clinical-skills education?

options.text: The nurse personally performs every complex procedure.
The nurse replaces simulation with policy review.
The nurse assesses technical speed only.
The nurse builds reliable competency systems that develop judgement, feedback and safe help-seeking.

questions.rationale: Level 3 leadership strengthens the capability of others and the learning system. Section 2 - Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems

questions.stem: Repeated specimen-labelling errors occur because labels print away from the bedside and several patients have similar names. Which intervention is strongest?

options.text: Introduce bedside label printing, barcode verification and a redesigned workflow.
Remind staff to check labels carefully.
Ask patients to inspect their labels.

questions.rationale: Workflow redesign and forcing functions are stronger than reminders alone.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects human-factors thinking?

options.text: Competent staff should never make mistakes.
Systems should reduce reliance on perfect memory, attention and concentration.
Errors are mainly caused by poor motivation.

questions.rationale: Human performance is limited, especially under fatigue and interruption.

questions.stem: A medication-preparation area is frequently interrupted. What is the strongest control?

options.text: Redesign the area and workflow to reduce interruptions during high-risk tasks.
Ask nurses to prepare medicines faster.

questions.rationale: Environmental and workflow redesign is stronger than relying on vigilance.

questions.stem: Which recommendation is weakest after a procedural incident?

options.text: Tell staff to be more careful.

questions.rationale: General reminders are weak controls because they rely on memory and attention.

questions.stem: Why should frontline staff participate in learning reviews?

options.text: They understand how work is actually performed and where pressures or workarounds occur.
They can identify who is to blame.

questions.rationale: Frontline insight helps reveal practical system conditions.

questions.stem: A review blames one nurse for using the wrong connector but ignores two nearly identical connectors stored together. What is missing?

options.text: Analysis of equipment design and storage as contributing system factors.

questions.rationale: Systems thinking examines conditions that shaped the error.

questions.stem: Which control is strongest in the hierarchy of controls?

options.text: A connector design that makes incorrect attachment physically impossible.

questions.rationale: Forcing functions and engineering controls are stronger than administrative reminders.

questions.stem: A procedure kit contains different items on each ward. What is the most appropriate improvement?

options.text: Ask staff to memorise local differences.
Allow each ward to continue its preference.
Standardise kit contents and layout across the service where clinically appropriate.

questions.rationale: Standardisation reduces variation and omissions.

questions.stem: A new checklist increases completion time and staff begin bypassing it. What should leaders do?

options.text: Review usability, workflow impact and whether the checklist targets meaningful risks.

questions.rationale: Workarounds may signal poor design and should prompt evaluation.

questions.stem: Which question best supports a systems learning review?

options.text: What happened, how did conditions shape the event and what controls could reduce recurrence?
Which staff member should be retrained?

questions.rationale: Learning reviews should focus on how and why, not blame alone.

questions.stem: A service standardises infusion pumps but leaves programming terminology inconsistent. What risk remains?

options.text: Cognitive confusion and programming error due to inconsistent language.

questions.rationale: Standardisation should include interfaces, labels and terminology.

questions.stem: Which finding suggests alert fatigue?

options.text: Staff respond promptly to critical alerts.
Staff frequently override or ignore alerts because many are non-actionable.

questions.rationale: Excessive low-value alerts can desensitise users.

questions.stem: A review produces ten broad recommendations with no owners or deadlines. What is the main problem?

options.text: Recommendations are unlikely to be implemented or evaluated.
Owners are unnecessary in team-based work.

questions.rationale: Recommendations should be specific, assigned and evaluated.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective standardisation?

options.text: Every ward uses identical documentation regardless of context.
Variation and omissions decrease while appropriate clinical judgement remains possible.

questions.rationale: Good standardisation supports reliability without eliminating judgement.

questions.stem: A procedure error occurs after 14 hours of work. What factor should be examined?

options.text: Fatigue and workload as human-factors contributors.

questions.rationale: Fatigue affects attention, memory and decision-making.

questions.stem: Which intervention best addresses similar-name patient risk?

options.text: Ask staff to remember the names.
Assign patients to different rooms only.
Use prominent alerts, two-identifier verification and barcode confirmation.

questions.rationale: Multiple system controls reduce reliance on memory.

questions.stem: A standard pathway is introduced but equipment remains unavailable on night shift. What should leaders conclude?

options.text: Implementation conditions are incomplete and reliability will remain poor.

questions.rationale: Safe processes require resources as well as written standards.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects a strong learning review?

options.text: Specific changes are implemented and shown to reduce the identified risk.

questions.rationale: The purpose of review is measurable risk reduction.

questions.stem: What is the main value of a forcing function?

options.text: It prevents or makes an unsafe action difficult to complete.

questions.rationale: Forcing functions reduce reliance on memory and voluntary compliance.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 3 systems leadership?

options.text: The nurse personally corrects staff errors.
The nurse increases education after every incident.
The nurse removes all local variation.
The nurse redesigns conditions so safe procedural performance is easier and more reliable.

questions.rationale: Level 3 leadership focuses on system design and reliable practice. Section 3 - Quality Improvement and Clinical-Skills Governance

questions.stem: A ward has frequent peripheral IV failures. What should the improvement team do first?

options.text: Define the problem using baseline data and review insertion, securement, site selection and daily assessment.
Retrain all staff before analysing the pattern.

questions.rationale: Improvement begins with a clearly defined problem and understanding of current practice.

questions.stem: Which is a process measure for an IV improvement project?

options.text: Percentage of insertions using the standard securement and assessment bundle.

questions.rationale: Process measures show whether the intended practice occurred.

questions.stem: Which is an outcome measure for the same project?

options.text: Rate of infiltration, phlebitis or early device failure.

questions.rationale: Outcome measures describe the effect on patients or devices.

questions.stem: Which is a balancing measure?

options.text: Additional procedure time or workload created by the new bundle.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures identify unintended consequences.

questions.stem: A quality project improves checklist completion but patient pain remains unchanged. What should leaders conclude?

options.text: Process compliance has improved, but the intervention has not yet improved the patient outcome.
Pain is unrelated to procedural quality.

questions.rationale: Process improvement should be linked to meaningful outcomes and experience.

questions.stem: Which governance elements support safe clinical procedures?

options.text: Policies, credentialing, competency records, equipment maintenance, incident review and audit.

questions.rationale: Clinical-skills governance requires multiple organisational controls.

questions.stem: A policy remains current, but the approved equipment is no longer available. What should leaders do?

options.text: Review the procedure, equipment, training and policy together before continued use.
Remove the policy from the intranet.

questions.rationale: Governance requires alignment between policy, equipment and competence.

questions.stem: Which patient-experience measures are relevant to procedural quality?
questions.rationale: The notes specifically identify pain, dignity, explanation and confidence.

questions.stem: A team wants to test a new wound-care bundle. What is the best approach?

options.text: Test a focused change in a small setting, study results and adapt before wider rollout.
Change multiple processes simultaneously without measurement.

questions.rationale: Small improvement cycles allow learning before scale-up.

questions.stem: Which audit finding most clearly indicates a governance gap?

options.text: Different staff use slightly different words when explaining a procedure.
High-risk procedures are performed by staff without current competency records.
One patient asks an additional question.
A procedure takes longer than expected.

questions.rationale: High-risk practice without verified competence is a significant governance failure.

questions.stem: A service introduces a procedural bundle and sees fewer infections but more treatment delays. What should happen?

options.text: Review the balancing measure and adapt the bundle to preserve benefit while reducing delay.

questions.rationale: Quality improvement should consider both benefits and unintended effects.

questions.stem: Which data source can identify procedural variation?

options.text: Audit, incident reports, equipment records, patient outcomes and experience.

questions.rationale: Multiple sources provide a fuller picture of quality and reliability.

questions.stem: A service measures hand hygiene but not infection outcomes. What is missing?
questions.rationale: Hand hygiene is a process measure; infection rates help evaluate patient impact.

questions.stem: Which action best links governance with frontline learning?

options.text: Use audit data and involve staff who perform the procedure in testing improvements.

questions.rationale: Frontline participation improves feasibility and implementation.

questions.stem: A new procedure is introduced without equipment-maintenance arrangements. What is the main risk?

options.text: Staff may prefer the old procedure.
Reliability and safety may decline when devices are unavailable or malfunction.

questions.rationale: Governance includes reliable equipment maintenance.

questions.stem: Which result best demonstrates sustainable improvement?

options.text: Improved outcomes maintained over time with acceptable workload and patient experience.

questions.rationale: Sustainability requires durable benefit without unacceptable burden.

questions.stem: A ward has a high fall rate during toileting transfers. What should the team examine?

options.text: Assessment, equipment, staffing, timing, environment and communication.

questions.rationale: Procedural outcomes are often shaped by multiple system factors.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes clinical-skills governance?

options.text: It ensures every nurse uses identical technique.
It provides organisational oversight so procedures are supported by current standards, competent staff, reliable equipment and monitoring.
It applies only to new procedures.

questions.rationale: Governance creates the structures that support safe practice.

questions.stem: A project shows no improvement after implementation. What should the team do?

options.text: Study the data, identify barriers and adapt or discontinue the change.

questions.rationale: Improvement cycles depend on learning and adaptation.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 3 quality leadership?

options.text: The nurse uses data, governance and patient experience to improve procedural reliability and outcomes.

questions.rationale: Level 3 practice integrates oversight, measurement and improvement. Section 4 - Digital Technology, Innovation and Global Skills Development

questions.stem: A virtual simulation programme improves test scores but learners still struggle with hands-on device setup. What should leaders do?

options.text: Use virtual simulation for preparation and reflection while retaining supervised hands-on practice.
Replace all practical training with virtual simulation.
Increase the number of online quizzes.

questions.rationale: Digital simulation complements but does not replace supervised physical practice.

questions.stem: Which risk is associated with electronic checklists?

options.text: Incorrect data, alert fatigue and workarounds may create new risks.
They remove the need for judgement.

questions.rationale: Digital support can reduce omission but also introduce automation-related hazards.

questions.stem: A barcode system frequently fails and staff bypass it. What should leaders do?

options.text: Investigate reliability, workflow and user experience, then redesign the system and contingency process.

questions.rationale: Workarounds often signal usability or reliability problems.

questions.stem: Which measure best evaluates a digital skills tool?

options.text: Safety, usability, learning performance, access, unintended effects and user experience.

questions.rationale: Digital tools require balanced evaluation beyond uptake.

questions.stem: A rural training programme depends on live video, but internet access is unreliable. What is the best response?

options.text: Add downloadable modules, local practice kits and remote coaching options.

questions.rationale: Equitable design provides alternatives for limited connectivity.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects automation bias?

options.text: Accepting a digital recommendation despite contradictory clinical evidence.

questions.rationale: Automation bias occurs when technology is trusted over professional judgement.

questions.stem: A digital checklist produces frequent non-actionable alerts. What should leaders do?

options.text: Ask users to ignore low-priority alerts.
Review thresholds and workflow to reduce alert fatigue while preserving critical warnings.

questions.rationale: Excessive alerts can reduce attention to important signals.

questions.stem: Which action best supports digital equity?

options.text: Require all learners to use the same technology.
Exclude learners unable to use the platform.
Provide alternatives for limited connectivity, equipment or digital literacy.

questions.rationale: Access barriers should be addressed so technology does not exclude learners.

questions.stem: A global clinical-skills package uses equipment unavailable locally. What should leaders do?

options.text: Adapt the training and workflow to local equipment, scope, regulation and resources.
Purchase the equipment before reviewing need.

questions.rationale: Global standards should be adapted to local context.

questions.stem: Which feature is essential when introducing decision support?

options.text: Clear accountability, override processes and monitoring for error or bias.

questions.rationale: Digital support must be governed and critically monitored.

questions.stem: A video-review system is introduced for skill assessment. What ethical issue requires attention?

options.text: Consent, privacy, secure storage and appropriate access.

questions.rationale: Recorded clinical performance creates privacy and governance obligations.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates successful blended education?

options.text: Learners gain knowledge remotely and demonstrate safe hands-on competence under supervision.

questions.rationale: Blended learning should connect digital preparation with verified practical performance.

questions.stem: A digital tool performs well in one country but poorly in another. What should leaders investigate?

options.text: Differences in workflow, equipment, language, regulation and digital infrastructure.

questions.rationale: Technology performance depends on local context.

questions.stem: Which global collaboration approach is most sustainable?

options.text: Sharing core safety standards while co-designing local adaptation and building local capability.

questions.rationale: Sustainable collaboration combines shared learning with local ownership.

questions.stem: A virtual-reality programme is highly realistic but causes motion sickness and excludes some users. What should leaders do?

options.text: Continue because realism is the priority.
Evaluate usability and provide alternative learning methods.

questions.rationale: Safety and accessibility are part of technology evaluation.

questions.stem: Which factor should be included in a digital downtime plan?

options.text: A promise that the system will rarely fail.
A tested alternative for communication, records and essential processes.

questions.rationale: Downtime planning preserves continuity when technology fails.

questions.stem: A decision-support prompt conflicts with an experienced nurse’s assessment. What should happen?

options.text: Verify data, use clinical judgement and escalate the discrepancy appropriately.

questions.rationale: Technology supports but does not replace professional judgement.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates equitable global skills development?

options.text: Every learner uses the same platform.
Learners across settings can access adapted education and demonstrate competence despite resource differences.
Training remains dependent on international faculty.

questions.rationale: Equity focuses on meaningful access and locally sustainable capability.

questions.stem: How should video review be used most effectively?

options.text: As the sole evidence of competence.
As a reflective and feedback tool alongside direct observation and supervised practice.

questions.rationale: Video supports reflection but should be part of a broader assessment process.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 3 innovation leadership?

options.text: The nurse introduces the newest technology.
The nurse replaces supervision with digital tools.
The nurse evaluates technology critically, protects access and safety, and adapts global learning to local context.

questions.rationale: Level 3 leadership combines innovation, governance, equity and contextual adaptation.
